idiom_name: std::thread scheduler loop + std::queue of std::packaged_task
implementation_notes: The default modern C++ realization: the proxy wraps each servant call in a std::packaged_task, pushes it onto a std::queue guarded by std::mutex/std::condition_variable, and returns the std::future obtained from get_future(); a dedicated std::thread pops and executes tasks, so only that thread touches the servant and no locks are needed inside it. std::async exists but leaves the execution policy unspecified, so a dedicated scheduler thread is the predictable form; use it when Asio or ACE are not already in the stack.
pitfalls: std::packaged_task is move-only: it needs std::queue<std::packaged_task<..>> or a heap wrapper; std::function cannot store it.
std::future::get() blocks; calling it from the scheduler thread (for example inside another method request) is an immediate self-deadlock.
Exceptions land in the future and only surface at get(); a future that nobody reads silently swallows the failure.

variants.name: Boost.Asio strand + post() method requests
variants.implementation_notes: When Asio already drives the application, the io_context is the activation queue and the scheduler, and a strand gives the servant its serialization guarantee: Asio defines a strand as a strictly sequential invocation of its event handlers, with no concurrent invocation, so posting a method request to the servant's strand replaces both the request queue and the servant's locking. The proxy posts a handler that captures the arguments plus a std::promise and returns its future; every servant member runs only inside strand-bound handlers.
pitfalls: A strand serializes handlers, not threads: shared state touched outside the strand still races, so every access must be posted through the same strand.
Blocking inside a strand handler - including waiting on the returned future - stalls all handlers on that strand and can deadlock the io_context.
Handler captures must outlive the post; objects owned by the handler need shared ownership or an executor-aware guard.

variants.name: ACE Method Request / Activation Queue / Future (classic reference)
variants.implementation_notes: The pattern's home implementation ships with ACE and is the one shown in the pattern's own documentation: subclasses of ACE_Method_Request carry each method's guard() and call(), ACE_Activation_Queue is the request buffer, an ACE_Task-based scheduler thread runs the dequeue/dispatch loop, and ACE_Future carries results back through the proxy. Choose it only when ACE's service-configuration and threading layers are already part of the system, since it pulls in ACE's task and policy machinery.
pitfalls: Method requests are heap-allocated and must be deleted or reference-counted along the scheduler path; the leak is silent until load rises.
ACE's own threads and policies must not be mixed casually with another framework's threading: the synchronization the pattern hides comes back at the seams.
